cards.q: Which membrane protein forms a continuous water filled pore that a solute passes through without binding to a transport site?
cards.a: A channel protein.
options: A carrier protein
A channel protein
An ATP driven pump
A membrane receptor
cards.explanation: A channel protein lines an aqueous pore, so solute flows through without a binding and release step. A carrier binds the solute and changes shape to deliver it, which is slower. A pump also binds solute but spends ATP to move it uphill. A receptor binds a ligand to start a signal and does not carry the ligand across.

cards.q: What supplies the energy for facilitated diffusion of glucose into a cell?
cards.a: The concentration gradient of glucose itself.
options: Direct hydrolysis of ATP by the carrier
The concentration gradient of glucose itself
The Na+ gradient built by the Na+/K+ ATPase
Hydrolysis of GTP by a coupled G protein
cards.explanation: Facilitated diffusion is passive. The carrier only provides a path, and the glucose gradient does the work, so transport runs downhill and stops at equilibrium. Direct ATP use would make it primary active transport, and using the Na+ gradient would make it secondary active transport. GTP hydrolysis belongs to signaling proteins, not to GLUT carriers.

cards.q: A carrier moves D-glucose across the membrane but will not move L-glucose. Which property is this?
cards.a: Specificity.
options: Electrogenicity
Saturation
Competition
Specificity
cards.explanation: Specificity means the binding site fits some molecules and rejects others, which is why a mirror image sugar is turned away. Saturation is the plateau in rate when every site is busy. Competition happens when two molecules that both fit the site slow each other down. Electrogenicity refers to a transporter moving net charge, which this carrier does not.

cards.q: Which substance crosses the lipid bilayer most readily by simple diffusion, with no membrane protein required?
cards.a: Oxygen.
options: An amino acid
Glucose
Na+
Oxygen
cards.explanation: Oxygen is small and nonpolar, so it dissolves in the lipid core and crosses directly. Glucose and amino acids are polar and need carriers such as GLUT or amino acid transporters. Na+ carries a charge and drags a shell of water with it, so it needs a channel or a transporter and essentially never slips through the bilayer.

cards.q: The GLUT family of transporters moves glucose across a cell membrane by which mechanism?
cards.a: Facilitated diffusion.
options: Primary active transport
Secondary active transport
Facilitated diffusion
Simple diffusion through the bilayer
cards.explanation: GLUT proteins are carriers that let glucose move down its own gradient, which is facilitated diffusion. Primary active transport would require GLUT to hydrolyze ATP, and secondary active transport would require it to be coupled to Na+, which is true of SGLT but not of GLUT. Simple diffusion is ruled out because glucose is polar and needs the protein.

cards.q: During facilitated diffusion of an uncharged solute, net movement stops at which point?
cards.a: When the solute concentration is equal on both sides of the membrane.
options: When the solute concentration is equal on both sides of the membrane
When every carrier has completed one cycle
When the cell runs out of ATP
When the membrane potential reaches zero
cards.explanation: Passive transport stops when the driving gradient is gone, so net flux ends at equal concentrations even though single molecules keep moving both ways. Carriers are reusable and are not consumed by a cycle. ATP is irrelevant because the process is passive, and membrane potential drives charged solutes, not an uncharged one like glucose.

cards.q: What is the name for the maximum transport rate reached when every carrier binding site is occupied?
cards.a: Transport maximum.
options: Transport maximum
Permeability coefficient
Equilibrium potential
Renal threshold
cards.explanation: The transport maximum is the ceiling set by the number of carriers, and once it is reached, adding more solute does not speed transport. The renal threshold is the plasma concentration at which a solute first appears in urine, a related but different idea. The permeability coefficient describes how easily a substance crosses by simple diffusion, and the equilibrium potential is a voltage, not a rate.

cards.q: Gating refers to which property of a membrane channel?
cards.a: Opening and closing in response to a stimulus.
options: Binding one solute tightly and rejecting all others
Using ATP to move solute against its gradient
Opening and closing in response to a stimulus
Reversing direction when the gradient reverses
cards.explanation: A gated channel switches between open and closed states in response to voltage, a ligand, or mechanical stress, so the cell can control permeability moment to moment. Tight binding describes a carrier, not a channel pore. ATP use describes a pump. Reversing with the gradient is true of any passive pathway and is not what gating means.

cards.q: Extracellular glucose is raised from a very low value to twice that value while the GLUT carriers remain far from saturated. What happens to the rate of glucose entry?
cards.a: It roughly doubles.
options: It roughly doubles
It jumps immediately to the transport maximum
It stays the same
It falls by about half
cards.explanation: Well below saturation most carriers are free, so the rate rises in near proportion to the gradient and doubling the outside concentration roughly doubles entry. The rate would only stay flat if the carriers were already saturated. Nothing here reduces the gradient, so a fall makes no sense, and the transport maximum is reached only when carrier sites are fully occupied.

cards.q: A cell is moved into a solution in which glucose is lower outside the cell than inside. Which way does GLUT move glucose?
cards.a: Out of the cell, down its concentration gradient.
options: Neither way, because a carrier needs ATP to run in reverse
Into the cell until the concentrations are equal
Into the cell, because carriers only work inward
Out of the cell, down its concentration gradient
cards.explanation: A facilitated diffusion carrier has no preferred direction. It simply follows the gradient, so with more glucose inside, net movement is outward. Carriers are not one way valves, and reversing does not cost ATP because no energy is being added in either direction. Inward movement would require glucose to climb its gradient, which passive transport cannot do.

cards.q: Galactose is added at high concentration to a cell taking up glucose through a carrier that binds both sugars. What happens to glucose uptake?
cards.a: It falls, because galactose occupies the shared binding sites.
options: It rises, because more total sugar is available
It is unchanged, because carriers handle only one sugar
It stops permanently
It falls, because galactose occupies the shared binding sites
cards.explanation: When two solutes fit the same site, they compete, and the more abundant one wins more cycles, so glucose uptake drops. Uptake does not rise because the number of carriers is fixed. It is not unchanged, because the premise says the carrier binds both sugars. The block is not permanent either, since raising glucose again would win back sites.

cards.q: Doubling the oxygen concentration outside a cell doubles the rate of oxygen entry, and the rate keeps climbing with no plateau at any concentration tested. Which process is this?
cards.a: Simple diffusion.
options: Simple diffusion
Facilitated diffusion
Primary active transport
Secondary active transport
cards.explanation: A rate that keeps rising in direct proportion with no ceiling means there is no limited number of binding sites, which is the signature of simple diffusion through the lipid. Facilitated diffusion would plateau once carriers were saturated. Both active transport types would plateau as well and would also require an energy source, which a gas moving downhill does not use.

cards.q: A treatment denatures every carrier protein in a cell membrane. Which solute still crosses at nearly its original rate?
cards.a: A steroid hormone.
options: A steroid hormone
Fructose
Glucose
An amino acid
cards.explanation: Steroid hormones are lipid soluble and dissolve straight through the bilayer, so losing carriers barely affects them. Glucose and fructose both depend on GLUT family carriers, and amino acids depend on their own carrier proteins, so all three would slow sharply. The general rule is that only small nonpolar or lipid soluble molecules are carrier independent.

cards.q: Solute A enters a cell at a rate that rises in a straight line as its concentration rises. Solute B enters at a rate that rises and then levels off. What does the plateau for solute B indicate?
cards.a: The carriers for solute B are saturated.
options: Solute B has reached equilibrium across the membrane
All the channels for solute B have closed
The carriers for solute B are saturated
Solute B is being pumped uphill with ATP
cards.explanation: A plateau means the transport proteins are the limiting factor, so every binding site is occupied and adding solute cannot speed things up. It does not imply ATP use, since facilitated diffusion saturates too. Equilibrium is ruled out because the outside concentration is being raised and net entry continues. Closed channels would drop the rate to near zero rather than hold it at a steady maximum.

cards.q: Ions cross through a single open channel at a far higher rate than solutes cross through a single carrier. What accounts for the difference?
cards.a: The channel does not need a conformational change for each ion.
options: The channel does not need a conformational change for each ion
The carrier binds only one solute at a time by chance
The carrier moves solute against its gradient
The channel is coupled to ATP hydrolysis
cards.explanation: An open channel is a pore, and ions stream through in single file with no cycle to complete, while a carrier must bind, change shape, release, and reset for every molecule. That cycling is the rate limiting step. Channels do not use ATP. Carriers do bind one solute at a time, but that is a consequence of the cycle rather than the cause, and facilitated carriers do not move solute uphill.

cards.q: Insulin causes a muscle cell to insert many more GLUT4 carriers into its membrane. Extracellular glucose is held constant at a level high enough to saturate the carriers already present. Predict the effect on glucose uptake and on the transport rate curve.
cards.a: Uptake rises and the maximum rate of the curve rises.
options: Uptake is unchanged because the existing carriers are saturated
Uptake falls because the new carriers compete for glucose
Uptake rises and the maximum rate of the curve rises
Uptake rises but the maximum rate of the curve is unchanged
cards.explanation: The maximum rate is set by how many carriers are in the membrane, so adding carriers raises the ceiling and uptake climbs even at a saturating concentration. The maximum cannot stay fixed while carrier number changes, since that ceiling is exactly what carrier number determines. Saturation limits the old carriers, not the new ones, and carriers in the same membrane do not compete with each other in a way that lowers total flux.

cards.q: A student measures uptake of a solute and finds three things: the rate plateaus at high concentration, a metabolic poison that removes ATP does not change the rate, and net uptake stops once the concentrations are equal on both sides. Which transport process is this?
cards.a: Facilitated diffusion.
options: Secondary active transport
Primary active transport
Simple diffusion
Facilitated diffusion
cards.explanation: The plateau shows a limited number of transport proteins, and stopping at equal concentrations shows the process is passive, which together define facilitated diffusion. Simple diffusion is ruled out because it would not plateau. Primary active transport is ruled out by the ATP result. Secondary active transport is ruled out because it can keep pushing solute uphill past the point of equal concentration.

cards.q: A mutation lowers the affinity of a glucose carrier for glucose but does not change how many carriers are in the membrane. Compare uptake at low glucose with uptake at very high glucose.
cards.a: Uptake is reduced at low glucose but the maximum rate is nearly normal.
options: Uptake is higher at low glucose and the maximum rate is unchanged
Uptake is reduced at every concentration, including at the maximum rate
Uptake is unchanged at low glucose but the maximum rate is lower
Uptake is reduced at low glucose but the maximum rate is nearly normal
cards.explanation: Affinity determines how readily glucose binds, so at low concentrations fewer carriers are loaded and uptake drops. Flooding the system with glucose overcomes weak binding, so the ceiling, which depends on carrier number rather than affinity, is nearly normal. The maximum falls only if carriers are lost or inhibited in a way that flooding cannot overcome, and lower affinity can never raise uptake.

cards.q: A red blood cell takes up glucose through a carrier. When a nonmetabolized glucose analog is added at equal concentration, glucose uptake falls by about half, and raising glucose alone restores uptake nearly to its original value. What does this show about the carrier?
cards.a: It is saturable and the two sugars compete for the same binding site.
options: It is a wide channel that both sugars flow through freely
It is saturable and the two sugars compete for the same binding site
It uses ATP that the analog consumes
It has been permanently destroyed by the analog
cards.explanation: Both sugars fit the same limited set of binding sites, so they share cycles and uptake of each falls. The fact that extra glucose wins the sites back shows the interference is reversible competition, not damage. If the analog destroyed the carrier, raising glucose would not help. ATP is not involved in facilitated diffusion, and a freely permeable wide pore would show no competition at all.

cards.q: How many K+ ions does the Na+/K+ ATPase bring into the cell per transport cycle?
cards.a: Two.
options: One
Two
Three
Four
cards.explanation: Each cycle imports two K+ while exporting three Na+, so more positive charge leaves than enters. Three is the Na+ number, not the K+ number, and mixing the two up is the most common error with this pump. One and four do not match the stoichiometry and would not give the pump its small direct contribution to the resting membrane potential.

cards.q: How many molecules of ATP does the Na+/K+ ATPase hydrolyze per transport cycle?
cards.a: One.
options: Five
One
Two
Three
cards.explanation: One ATP powers one full cycle, which moves three Na+ out and two K+ in. Two and three are the ion counts, not the ATP count, so they are easy to grab by mistake. Five is the total number of ions moved per cycle and again is not the ATP requirement.

cards.q: The Na+/K+ ATPase is called electrogenic. What does that mean?
cards.a: It moves net positive charge out of the cell each cycle.
options: It moves equal charge in each direction
It generates ATP as ions move down their gradients
It moves net positive charge out of the cell each cycle
It is activated by changes in membrane voltage
cards.explanation: Three positive charges leave and two enter, so each cycle exports one net positive charge and makes a small direct contribution to the negative resting potential. Being activated by voltage describes a voltage gated channel, not this pump. Equal charge exchange would make the pump electroneutral, which the three to two ratio rules out. The pump consumes ATP rather than making it.

cards.q: Which pair of gradients does the Na+/K+ ATPase maintain?
cards.a: Na+ high outside the cell and K+ high inside.
options: Ca2+ high outside and Na+ high inside
K+ high outside and Cl- high inside
Na+ high outside the cell and K+ high inside
Na+ high inside the cell and K+ high outside
cards.explanation: The pump pushes Na+ out and K+ in, so at rest Na+ is concentrated in the extracellular fluid and K+ is concentrated in the cytosol. The reversed version of that statement is the classic mix up and would give the wrong resting potential entirely. Ca2+ is indeed low inside, but it is handled by calcium pumps and exchangers, and Cl- is not a substrate of this pump.

cards.q: What makes the Na+/K+ ATPase an example of primary active transport?
cards.a: It hydrolyzes ATP directly to move ions against their gradients.
options: It hydrolyzes ATP directly to move ions against their gradients
It uses the Na+ gradient to move another solute uphill
It moves ions down their gradients through a pore
It works only when a hormone binds to it
cards.explanation: Primary means the transporter itself splits ATP and uses that energy immediately, which is exactly what this pump does for both ions. Using an existing Na+ gradient describes secondary active transport, such as SGLT. Downhill movement through a pore is a channel. Hormone dependence is a regulatory detail and is not part of the definition of primary active transport.

cards.q: Which drug class inhibits the Na+/K+ ATPase?
cards.a: Cardiac glycosides such as digoxin and ouabain.
options: Loop diuretics such as furosemide
Beta blockers such as propranolol
Cardiac glycosides such as digoxin and ouabain
Calcium channel blockers such as verapamil
cards.explanation: Cardiac glycosides bind the extracellular face of the pump and lock it, which is why they are the standard experimental tool for stopping Na+ and K+ pumping. Beta blockers act on adrenergic receptors, calcium channel blockers act on voltage gated Ca2+ channels, and loop diuretics block the Na+/K+/2Cl- symporter in the loop of Henle. All three act on proteins other than this pump.

cards.q: In the pump cycle, phosphorylation of the Na+/K+ ATPase by ATP does what?
cards.a: Changes the pump's shape so the Na+ sites face outward and release Na+.
options: Changes the pump's shape so the Na+ sites face outward and release Na+
Attaches K+ to the pump so it can be carried inward
Blocks the pump until a hormone removes the phosphate
Opens a permanent pore through the pump
cards.explanation: Adding the phosphate group drives a conformational change that swings the loaded Na+ sites to the outside and lowers their affinity, so Na+ is dropped into the extracellular fluid. The pump never forms an open pore, since that would let ions leak back down their gradients. K+ binds after the shape change, not because of phosphorylation, and dephosphorylation happens as part of the normal cycle rather than by hormone control.

cards.q: Roughly what fraction of a typical resting cell's ATP use is spent on the Na+/K+ ATPase?
cards.a: About 25 percent.
options: About 90 percent
About 1 percent
About 5 percent
About 25 percent
cards.explanation: Around a quarter of resting ATP consumption goes to this pump in a typical cell, and the share is even higher in neurons and kidney tubule cells, which is why these tissues fail fast without oxygen. One and five percent badly understate a continuous cost the cell pays every second to hold its gradients. Ninety percent leaves nothing for synthesis, contraction, or signaling, which cells clearly perform.

cards.q: Ouabain is applied to a cell. Predict what happens to intracellular Na+ over the next several minutes.
cards.a: It rises, because Na+ leaks in and is no longer pumped out.
options: It rises, because Na+ leaks in and is no longer pumped out
It falls, because Na+ leaks out unopposed
It is unchanged, because the membrane is impermeable to Na+
It rises briefly and then returns to normal
cards.explanation: Na+ constantly leaks inward down a steep electrochemical gradient, and the pump is the only thing removing it, so blocking the pump lets Na+ pile up inside. It cannot fall, because there is no other route that carries Na+ out against the gradient. The membrane is leaky to Na+, not impermeable, and nothing restores the gradient while the pump stays blocked.

cards.q: A cell's Na+/K+ ATPase is blocked. What is the immediate effect on the resting membrane potential, before the ion gradients have had time to run down?
cards.a: A small depolarization of a few mV.
options: A small depolarization of a few mV
A small hyperpolarization of a few mV
No change at all under any circumstances
A large hyperpolarization of about 30 mV
cards.explanation: The pump exports one net positive charge per cycle, so it contributes a few mV of negativity directly. Removing that contribution makes the inside slightly less negative, a small depolarization. Losing an outward positive current cannot hyperpolarize the cell. The larger change comes later, as the K+ and Na+ gradients themselves decay, so saying nothing changes ignores both the direct and the delayed effect.

cards.q: Intracellular Na+ rises in a working nerve cell after a burst of action potentials. What happens to the rate of the Na+/K+ ATPase?
cards.a: It speeds up, because intracellular Na+ is the substrate that loads the pump.
options: It slows, because Na+ inhibits the pump
It stops until Na+ returns to baseline
It speeds up, because intracellular Na+ is the substrate that loads the pump
It is unaffected, because pump rate depends only on ATP
cards.explanation: Na+ inside the cell binds the pump's cytoplasmic sites, so more Na+ means more loaded pumps and a faster cycling rate. That is the built in feedback that restores gradients after activity. Na+ is a substrate, not an inhibitor, so slowing or stopping is backward. ATP matters, but at normal ATP levels the internal Na+ concentration is the variable that sets the pace.

cards.q: The Ca2+ ATPase of the sarcoplasmic reticulum hydrolyzes ATP to move Ca2+ from the cytosol into the SR against its gradient. How is this transporter classified?
cards.a: Primary active transport.
options: Simple diffusion
Primary active transport
Facilitated diffusion
Secondary active transport
cards.explanation: The transporter itself splits ATP to drive uphill movement, which is the definition of primary active transport, the same category as the Na+/K+ ATPase. Secondary active transport would use an existing ion gradient rather than ATP, as the sodium calcium exchanger does. Both diffusion categories are passive and could never build a thousandfold Ca2+ gradient across the SR membrane.

cards.q: A cell is deprived of oxygen and its ATP level falls sharply. Predict what happens to cell volume.
cards.a: The cell swells, because Na+ accumulates inside and water follows.
options: The cell shrinks, because Na+ leaves and water follows it out
The volume holds steady, because the membrane is impermeable to water
The cell shrinks, because K+ is pumped in and drags water out
The cell swells, because Na+ accumulates inside and water follows
cards.explanation: Without ATP the pump stops, Na+ leaks in faster than K+ leaks out, and the added intracellular solute raises osmolarity so water follows and the cell swells. Shrinking would require solute to leave, which is the opposite of what a failed pump allows. Membranes are quite water permeable, and pumping K+ in requires the very ATP the cell no longer has.

cards.q: Extracellular K+ falls well below normal in a tissue bath. What is the immediate effect on Na+/K+ ATPase activity?
cards.a: It slows, because external K+ is needed to load the pump's outward facing sites.
options: It rises, because the K+ gradient is steeper
It slows, because external K+ is needed to load the pump's outward facing sites
It is unchanged, because the pump responds only to Na+
It stops entirely and cannot restart
cards.explanation: The pump needs K+ bound on the outside to complete its cycle, so lowering external K+ leaves those sites empty and slows the whole pump. A steeper gradient does not help, because a pump works against gradients rather than being driven by them. Internal Na+ is one substrate but not the only one, and the slowdown is graded and reversible rather than a permanent stop.

cards.q: Which statement correctly describes the direction each ion moves relative to its own concentration gradient during one pump cycle?
cards.a: Both Na+ and K+ move up their gradients.
options: Both Na+ and K+ move up their gradients
Both Na+ and K+ move down their gradients
Na+ moves down its gradient and K+ moves up its gradient
Na+ moves up its gradient and K+ moves down its gradient
cards.explanation: Na+ is already high outside and is pushed further out, and K+ is already high inside and is pushed further in, so both ions are moved uphill and that is why ATP is required. If either ion were moving downhill, that leg of the cycle would need no energy. If both moved downhill, the pump would be a channel and the gradients would collapse instead of being maintained.

cards.q: Digoxin partly inhibits the Na+/K+ ATPase in a cardiac muscle cell. Trace the consequence: what happens to intracellular Na+, and then to intracellular Ca2+ handled by the sodium calcium exchanger?
cards.a: Na+ rises, and Ca2+ rises because the exchanger has a weaker gradient to work with.
options: Na+ falls, and Ca2+ rises because Ca2+ replaces the missing Na+ inside
Na+ falls, and Ca2+ falls because both pumps are blocked together
Na+ rises, and Ca2+ rises because the exchanger has a weaker gradient to work with
Na+ rises, and Ca2+ falls because the exchanger works harder than before
cards.explanation: Blocking the pump lets Na+ build up inside, which flattens the inward Na+ gradient that the sodium calcium exchanger uses as its power source. With less driving force the exchanger removes less Ca2+, so intracellular Ca2+ rises and each contraction becomes stronger. Na+ cannot fall when its only exit is blocked, and the exchanger cannot work harder when the gradient driving it has shrunk.

cards.q: A neuron is deprived of oxygen for several minutes and ATP falls. Predict the sequence for the K+ gradient and then the membrane potential.
cards.a: K+ leaks out and is not replaced, so the potential drifts toward zero.
options: K+ is drawn inside by the pump reversing, so the potential becomes more negative
K+ is unchanged and the potential is set only by Cl-
K+ stays high inside and the potential becomes more negative
K+ leaks out and is not replaced, so the potential drifts toward zero
cards.explanation: With no ATP the pump cannot return the K+ that leaks out, so the K+ gradient dissipates, and since that gradient is the main source of the resting potential, the membrane depolarizes toward zero. The gradient cannot be preserved without pumping. A pump running backward to import K+ would still need energy input and does not happen here. Cl- distributes according to the potential in most cells rather than setting it.

cards.q: Red blood cells are stored cold for hours. They gain Na+ and lose K+. They are then rewarmed to 37 C with glucose available, and the normal gradients are restored. What best explains both halves of this result?
cards.a: Cold slowed pump activity, and warming with fuel restored ATP supply and pumping.
options: Cold slowed pump activity, and warming with fuel restored ATP supply and pumping
Cold reversed the pump, and warming reversed it back
Cold destroyed the pumps, and warming caused new pumps to be synthesized in minutes
Cold opened Na+ channels, and warming closed them
cards.explanation: Cold slows metabolism and the pump much more than it slows passive leak, so ions drift down their gradients, and warming with glucose restores ATP so the pump can catch up and rebuild them. Gating of Na+ channels by temperature is not what drives this classic result, and a pump does not run backward simply because it is cold. Synthesizing new pumps would take far longer than the rapid recovery seen here.

cards.q: An experimenter blocks the Na+/K+ ATPase and records membrane potential for an hour. The potential shifts by about 4 mV within seconds and then, over many minutes, drifts much further toward zero. What explains the two phases?
cards.a: The fast shift is loss of the pump's electrogenic current, and the slow drift is the gradients running down.
options: The fast shift is an action potential, and the slow drift is the cell repolarizing
The fast shift is loss of the pump's electrogenic current, and the slow drift is the gradients running down
The fast shift is the K+ gradient collapsing, and the slow drift is Cl- redistributing
Both phases reflect Ca2+ slowly entering the cell
cards.explanation: The pump exports net positive charge continuously, so removing it costs a few mV immediately. The much larger, slower change comes as Na+ leaks in and K+ leaks out with no pump to restore them, which erodes the gradients that generate the potential. Gradients cannot collapse in seconds given the small ion fluxes involved, and neither Ca2+ entry nor an action potential is described in this recording.

cards.q: In a symport, the two transported solutes move in which directions?
cards.a: Both in the same direction across the membrane.
options: Both move only when ATP is bound to the carrier
Both in the same direction across the membrane
In opposite directions across the membrane
One moves and the other stays bound to the carrier
cards.explanation: Symport, also called cotransport, carries both solutes the same way at once, as SGLT does when it brings Na+ and glucose into the cell together. Opposite directions define an antiport, such as the sodium calcium exchanger. A solute that stayed bound would never be delivered, and direct ATP binding would make the protein a primary active pump rather than a coupled carrier.

cards.q: In an antiport, the two transported solutes move in which directions?
cards.a: In opposite directions across the membrane.
options: Both into the cell
Both out of the cell
In opposite directions across the membrane
In the same direction, one after the other
cards.explanation: An antiport, also called an exchanger, moves one solute in while moving the other out, as the Na+/H+ exchanger does. Moving both the same way, whether in or out, describes a symport. Sequential same direction movement is still symport, since what defines antiport is opposing direction, not timing.

cards.q: Which ion's gradient directly powers SGLT, the sodium glucose cotransporter?
cards.a: The Na+ gradient.
options: The K+ gradient
The Na+ gradient
The Ca2+ gradient
The Cl- gradient
cards.explanation: Na+ is kept low inside the cell, so it has a steep inward electrochemical gradient, and SGLT harnesses that inward rush to drag glucose in with it. K+ is high inside, so its gradient points outward and cannot pull glucose in. Ca2+ and Cl- gradients exist but are not coupled to this carrier.

cards.q: The sodium calcium exchanger moves how many Na+ into the cell for each Ca2+ it moves out?
cards.a: Three.
options: Two
Three
Four
One
cards.explanation: Three Na+ enter for each Ca2+ that leaves, so the exchanger carries net positive charge inward and is electrogenic. One would not release enough energy to move Ca2+ out against its very steep gradient. Two is the K+ number for the Na+/K+ ATPase and is a common cross up. Four does not match the measured stoichiometry.

cards.q: The Na+/H+ exchanger brings Na+ into the cell while sending H+ out. How is it classified?
cards.a: Antiport.
options: Antiport
Primary active transport
Simple diffusion
Symport
cards.explanation: Opposite directions for the two solutes makes this an antiport, and because it runs on the Na+ gradient rather than on ATP, it is secondary active transport. A symport would carry both the same way. It is not primary active because the protein does not hydrolyze ATP. Simple diffusion would require no protein and could not move H+ uphill.

cards.q: What is the immediate energy source for secondary active transport?
cards.a: The electrochemical gradient of a driver ion, usually Na+.
options: GTP supplied by a G protein
Heat released by cell metabolism
ATP bound directly to the transporter
The electrochemical gradient of a driver ion, usually Na+
cards.explanation: The carrier lets one ion fall down its electrochemical gradient and uses that released energy to haul a second solute uphill, with no ATP touching the carrier itself. Direct ATP hydrolysis would make it primary active transport. GTP powers signaling proteins, and heat is not a usable energy source for directed transport in cells.

cards.q: Which pump ultimately supplies the energy that secondary active transport depends on?
cards.a: The Na+/K+ ATPase.
options: The proton pump of the stomach
The Ca2+ ATPase of the sarcoplasmic reticulum
The H+/K+ ATPase of the kidney
The Na+/K+ ATPase
cards.explanation: The Na+/K+ ATPase spends ATP to keep intracellular Na+ low, which creates the inward Na+ gradient that every Na+ coupled carrier taps. That is why secondary active transport is called secondary. The gastric proton pump and the renal H+/K+ ATPase acidify secretions but do not set up the cell's Na+ gradient. The SR Ca2+ ATPase fills the SR with Ca2+ and likewise does not power SGLT or the exchanger.

cards.q: SGLT moves Na+ and glucose into the cell together. Which category does SGLT belong to?
cards.a: Symport driven by the Na+ gradient.
options: Facilitated diffusion of glucose alone
Antiport driven by ATP
Symport driven by the Na+ gradient
Channel gated by glucose
cards.explanation: Both solutes cross in the same direction, which makes it a symport, and the driving force is the Na+ gradient rather than ATP, which makes it secondary active. Calling it an antiport reverses the geometry. It is not a channel, because the carrier binds both solutes and cycles through conformations. Facilitated diffusion of glucose alone describes GLUT, which cannot move glucose uphill.

cards.q: Extracellular Na+ is replaced with choline, an impermeant cation, in a bath containing intestinal cells. Predict glucose uptake through SGLT.
cards.a: It falls sharply, because the Na+ gradient that drives the carrier is gone.
options: It rises, because there is less competition for the carrier
It is unchanged, because glucose binds the carrier on its own
It falls sharply, because the Na+ gradient that drives the carrier is gone
It reverses, and glucose is pumped out of the cell
cards.explanation: SGLT only carries glucose when Na+ binds and moves inward down its gradient, so removing extracellular Na+ removes the driving force and uptake collapses. Na+ is a partner, not a competitor, so removing it cannot help. Glucose alone does not drive the cycle. Reversal would require a steep outward gradient for the driver ion, which choline cannot supply.

cards.q: A transporter in a cell membrane moves Cl- into the cell while moving HCO3- out. How should it be classified?
cards.a: Antiport.
options: Primary active transport
Channel mediated diffusion
Symport
Antiport
cards.explanation: Two solutes crossing in opposite directions is the definition of an antiport, no matter which ions are involved. A symport would move both the same way. Nothing states that the protein hydrolyzes ATP, so primary active transport is not supported. A channel carries one species through a pore and does not couple two solutes to each other.

cards.q: Glucose enters an intestinal cell through SGLT even though intracellular glucose is already higher than luminal glucose. How is that possible?
cards.a: Glucose is being carried uphill using energy released by Na+ moving downhill.
options: Glucose is being carried uphill using energy released by Na+ moving downhill
Glucose has become lipid soluble inside the cell
The carrier hydrolyzes ATP for each glucose molecule
The glucose gradient must actually be reversed
cards.explanation: Coupled transport only needs the total energy change to be favorable, so a steep inward Na+ gradient can pay for glucose climbing its own gradient. Glucose does not change its chemical nature inside the cell. SGLT never hydrolyzes ATP itself, which is what separates secondary from primary active transport. The premise states the glucose gradient, so denying it does not answer the question.

cards.q: The sodium calcium exchanger carries three Na+ in for each Ca2+ out. What is the net charge movement per cycle, and what does that do to the membrane potential?
cards.a: Net one positive charge inward, a slight depolarization.
options: Net two positive charges outward, a strong hyperpolarization
Net zero charge, no effect on potential
Net one positive charge inward, a slight depolarization
Net one positive charge outward, a slight hyperpolarization
cards.explanation: Three positive charges in and two positive charges out leave a net gain of one positive charge inside per cycle, which nudges the membrane potential toward less negative. Net zero would require the charges to balance, which three versus two does not. Any outward net movement reverses the actual direction, so the hyperpolarizing options describe the opposite of what happens.

cards.q: The Na+ gradient across a cell membrane is reduced by half. Predict the effect on Ca2+ export by the sodium calcium exchanger.
cards.a: Ca2+ export falls, so intracellular Ca2+ rises.
options: Ca2+ export rises, so intracellular Ca2+ falls
Ca2+ export falls, so intracellular Ca2+ rises
Ca2+ export is unchanged, because the exchanger uses ATP
Ca2+ export stops completely and cannot resume
cards.explanation: The exchanger is powered by Na+ falling into the cell, so a shallower Na+ gradient supplies less energy and less Ca2+ is pushed out, letting cytosolic Ca2+ climb. Export cannot rise when its driving force has shrunk. The exchanger does not use ATP directly, and a partial reduction in gradient slows the exchanger rather than halting it permanently.

cards.q: An amino acid is absorbed from the gut lumen by a Na+ coupled symporter. Removing Na+ from the lumen stops absorption. What does that experiment show?
cards.a: Absorption depends on the Na+ gradient, so it is secondary active.
options: Absorption depends on the Na+ gradient, so it is secondary active
The symporter hydrolyzes ATP directly for each amino acid
The amino acid uses the same carrier protein as glucose
The amino acid crosses the membrane by simple diffusion
cards.explanation: Absorption that fails without the driver ion identifies the Na+ gradient as the energy source, which is the definition of secondary active transport. Simple diffusion would be unaffected by removing Na+. Direct ATP use is not tested by this experiment and would make the carrier primary active. Sharing a carrier with glucose is a separate claim that removing Na+ does not address.

cards.q: A cell becomes acidic inside. The Na+/H+ exchanger responds by moving H+ out. Which gradient pays for moving H+ against its concentration gradient?
cards.a: The inward Na+ gradient.
options: The outward K+ gradient
The inward Cl- gradient
The outward HCO3- gradient
The inward Na+ gradient
cards.explanation: Na+ is far more concentrated outside than inside, so its inward movement releases energy the exchanger uses to push H+ out. K+ is concentrated inside, so its gradient points the wrong way to pull Na+ or H+ anywhere useful here. Cl- and HCO3- gradients drive other exchangers, such as the chloride bicarbonate antiport, but not this one.

cards.q: Ouabain is added to an intestinal epithelial cell. Trace the effect on intracellular Na+ and then on glucose uptake through SGLT at the apical membrane.
cards.a: Intracellular Na+ rises, the Na+ gradient shrinks, and SGLT glucose uptake falls.
options: Intracellular Na+ is unchanged, because SGLT keeps it low
Intracellular Na+ rises, the Na+ gradient shrinks, and SGLT glucose uptake falls
Intracellular Na+ rises, the Na+ gradient steepens, and SGLT glucose uptake rises
Intracellular Na+ falls, and SGLT glucose uptake rises
cards.explanation: Ouabain stops the Na+/K+ ATPase, so Na+ accumulates inside and the inward Na+ gradient flattens, which removes the energy source that SGLT depends on and glucose uptake slows. Rising internal Na+ makes the gradient shallower, not steeper, so that option contradicts itself. Na+ cannot fall with its only exit blocked, and SGLT brings Na+ into the cell rather than removing it.

cards.q: During ischemia a cardiac cell loses ATP, intracellular Na+ climbs, and the membrane depolarizes. The sodium calcium exchanger then begins running in reverse. What does reverse mode do, and what is the result?
cards.a: It brings Ca2+ into the cell and exports Na+, so intracellular Ca2+ rises to harmful levels.
options: It brings Ca2+ into the cell and imports more Na+, so both ions fall
It exports Ca2+ faster, so intracellular Ca2+ falls below normal
It stops all transport, so ion concentrations freeze where they are
It brings Ca2+ into the cell and exports Na+, so intracellular Ca2+ rises to harmful levels
cards.explanation: The exchanger has no fixed direction. It follows the combined Na+ gradient and membrane voltage, so when internal Na+ rises and the cell depolarizes, the favorable direction flips and Na+ leaves while Ca2+ enters, driving calcium overload. A transporter cannot move both coupled solutes inward at once. Faster export would require a steeper inward Na+ gradient, which ischemia destroys, and the exchanger keeps cycling rather than freezing.

cards.q: A drug blocks SGLT2 in the proximal tubule, so filtered glucose that would normally be reabsorbed stays in the tubular fluid. Predict the effect on urine glucose and on urine volume.
cards.a: Urine glucose rises and urine volume rises, because glucose holds water in the tubule.
options: Urine glucose rises and urine volume is unchanged, because water follows Na+ only
Urine glucose rises and urine volume rises, because glucose holds water in the tubule
Urine glucose rises and urine volume falls, because glucose absorbs water from the tubule
Urine glucose falls and urine volume rises
cards.explanation: Blocking the apical symporter leaves glucose in the tubular fluid, so it is excreted, and because the retained glucose is an osmotically active solute it holds water in the lumen and produces osmotic diuresis. Glucose in the lumen pulls water toward itself, so it cannot reduce urine volume. Glucose cannot fall when reabsorption is blocked, and water follows total osmotic gradients rather than Na+ alone.

cards.q: A student says that secondary active transport does not use ATP at all. What is the most accurate correction?
cards.a: The carrier uses no ATP, but the Na+ gradient it spends was built by an ATP driven pump.
options: The carrier hydrolyzes ATP slowly rather than quickly
The carrier uses ATP only when moving solute downhill
The claim is completely correct, since no ATP is involved anywhere in the process
The carrier uses no ATP, but the Na+ gradient it spends was built by an ATP driven pump
cards.explanation: Secondary active transporters never touch ATP, which is what makes them secondary, but they spend a gradient the Na+/K+ ATPase paid for with ATP, so the process is ATP dependent one step upstream. Slow hydrolysis by the carrier would make it primary active. A carrier does not need energy to move solute downhill. Saying no ATP is involved anywhere ignores that the gradient collapses within minutes if the pump stops.

cards.q: What does the transport maximum of a carrier mediated system represent?
cards.a: The highest transport rate possible once all carriers are saturated.
options: The rate at which the solute diffuses through the lipid bilayer
The rate at which the solute first appears in urine
The highest transport rate possible once all carriers are saturated
The concentration at which transport begins
cards.explanation: The transport maximum is the ceiling reached when every carrier binding site is occupied, so raising solute concentration further cannot speed transport. The concentration at which a solute first spills into urine is the renal threshold, a related idea measured in plasma units rather than rate units. Transport begins at any concentration above zero, and simple diffusion through lipid has no maximum at all.

cards.q: What physical feature of the membrane sets the value of the transport maximum?
cards.a: The number of functioning carrier proteins available.
options: The thickness of the lipid bilayer
The number of functioning carrier proteins available
The membrane potential
The temperature of the extracellular fluid
cards.explanation: Each carrier can only complete so many cycles per second, so the total ceiling is set by how many carriers are in the membrane. Bilayer thickness affects simple diffusion of lipid soluble substances, not carrier capacity. Membrane potential influences charged solutes but does not create or remove carriers. Temperature changes reaction rates broadly but is not what defines the maximum in a physiology curve.

cards.q: At about what plasma glucose concentration does glucose first begin to appear in the urine in a healthy adult?
cards.a: About 180 mg/dL.
options: About 400 mg/dL
About 80 mg/dL
About 120 mg/dL
About 180 mg/dL
cards.explanation: The renal threshold for glucose sits near 180 to 200 mg/dL, which is where the filtered load starts to exceed what some nephrons can reabsorb. Eighty and 120 mg/dL are ordinary fasting and fed values, so glucose is fully reabsorbed at both. By 400 mg/dL glucosuria is heavy and well past the point where it began.

cards.q: The transport maximum for glucose reabsorption in the kidney of a healthy adult is closest to which value?
cards.a: About 375 mg/min.
options: About 375 mg/min
About 1000 mg/min
About 125 mg/min
About 180 mg/min
cards.explanation: Roughly 375 mg/min is the standard figure for the combined capacity of the proximal tubule carriers. About 125 mg/min is the normal filtered load at a plasma glucose of 100 mg/dL, and 180 is the threshold expressed in mg/dL, so both numbers belong to different quantities in this same topic. A thousand mg/min far exceeds measured capacity.

cards.q: What is the term for glucose appearing in the urine?
cards.a: Glucosuria.
options: Glucosuria
Proteinuria
Hyperglycemia
Diuresis
cards.explanation: Glucosuria names glucose in the urine, which happens once the filtered load exceeds the transport maximum. Proteinuria is protein in the urine and points to a filtration barrier problem instead. Hyperglycemia is high glucose in the blood, which is the cause here rather than the urinary finding. Diuresis is an increased urine volume, which often accompanies glucosuria but is not the same term.

cards.q: How is the filtered load of a freely filtered solute such as glucose calculated?
cards.a: GFR multiplied by plasma concentration.
options: GFR multiplied by plasma concentration
GFR multiplied by urine concentration
Urine flow rate multiplied by plasma concentration
Plasma concentration divided by GFR
cards.explanation: Filtered load is the amount arriving in the tubule per minute, which is the volume filtered per minute times how much solute each volume carries, so GFR times plasma concentration. Dividing inverts the relationship and gives units that make no sense. Urine concentration reflects what escaped reabsorption, so it describes the excreted amount rather than the filtered amount.

cards.q: On a graph of glucose reabsorption rate against plasma glucose concentration, what does the curve do once the transport maximum is reached?
cards.a: It becomes flat at a constant rate.
options: It rises more steeply than before
It continues to rise in a straight line
It becomes flat at a constant rate
It falls back toward zero
cards.explanation: Once every carrier is occupied, reabsorption cannot go faster, so the curve flattens into a horizontal plateau while any extra filtered glucose is excreted. A continued straight line would describe simple diffusion, which has no carriers to saturate. The rate does not fall, because the carriers keep working at capacity, and it certainly cannot steepen after saturation.

cards.q: In renal glucose handling, what does the term splay describe?
cards.a: The gentle rounding of the curve between threshold and transport maximum.
options: The complete loss of reabsorption at high plasma glucose
The delay between filtration and excretion
The sudden vertical jump in excretion at the threshold
The gentle rounding of the curve between threshold and transport maximum
cards.explanation: Splay is the rounded shoulder in the curve, and it exists because nephrons differ in their filtered loads and carrier numbers, so some spill glucose before others do. A sharp vertical jump is what the curve would look like if every nephron were identical. Reabsorption is not lost at high plasma glucose, since it continues at the maximum rate, and splay is a shape, not a time delay.

cards.q: GFR is 125 mL/min and plasma glucose is 100 mg/dL. What is the filtered load of glucose?
cards.a: 125 mg/min.
options: 12.5 mg/min
125 mg/min
375 mg/min
1250 mg/min
cards.explanation: A plasma glucose of 100 mg/dL is 1 mg/mL, so 125 mL/min carries 125 mg/min into the tubule. The 12.5 value comes from slipping a decimal place during the dL to mL conversion. The 375 value is the transport maximum rather than the filtered load, and 1250 would require a plasma glucose ten times higher than the one given.

cards.q: GFR is 125 mL/min and plasma glucose is 400 mg/dL. The transport maximum for glucose is 375 mg/min. How much glucose is excreted per minute?
cards.a: 125 mg/min.
options: 500 mg/min
0 mg/min
125 mg/min
375 mg/min
cards.explanation: The filtered load is 4 mg/mL times 125 mL/min, or 500 mg/min, and the carriers can reclaim only 375 mg/min, so 125 mg/min is left in the tubule and excreted. Zero would require the filtered load to stay under the maximum. The 375 figure is what is reabsorbed, and 500 is what was filtered, so both are steps in the calculation rather than the answer.

cards.q: A person has a plasma glucose of 120 mg/dL with a normal GFR. Will glucose appear in the urine?
cards.a: No, because the filtered load is well below the transport maximum.
options: No, because the filtered load is well below the transport maximum
No, because glucose is too large to be filtered
Yes, because any glucose in plasma spills into urine
Yes, because 120 mg/dL exceeds the transport maximum
cards.explanation: At 120 mg/dL the filtered load is about 150 mg/min, comfortably under the 375 mg/min capacity, so the proximal tubule reclaims all of it. Plasma glucose is always present in the filtrate without spilling into urine, so the idea that any plasma glucose appears in urine is wrong on its face. The transport maximum is a rate, not a plasma concentration, so 120 mg/dL cannot exceed it. Glucose is small and is freely filtered.

cards.q: An experimental treatment doubles the number of glucose carriers in the proximal tubule. Predict the effect on the transport maximum for glucose.
cards.a: It roughly doubles.
options: It roughly doubles
It is halved
It is unchanged, because the maximum depends on GFR
It falls to zero, because carriers interfere with each other
cards.explanation: The maximum is the sum of what all carriers can move per minute, so doubling the carriers roughly doubles the ceiling. Halving is the opposite of adding capacity. GFR determines how much glucose arrives, not how much the carriers can handle, so the maximum is not fixed by GFR. Carriers work independently and do not disable one another.

cards.q: A person has a steady plasma glucose of 300 mg/dL with a GFR of 125 mL/min and a normal transport maximum of 375 mg/min. What is the rate of glucose reabsorption?
cards.a: 375 mg/min, the transport maximum.
options: 0 mg/min
125 mg/min
375 mg/min, the transport maximum
300 mg/min
cards.explanation: The filtered load is 3 mg/mL times 125 mL/min, or 375 mg/min, which exactly matches capacity, so the carriers reabsorb at the maximum and essentially nothing is excreted. The 125 value would be the filtered load at a normal plasma glucose. The 300 figure is the plasma concentration in different units and is not a rate. Reabsorption cannot be zero while functioning carriers are present.

cards.q: On a renal glucose curve, the excretion line stays at zero and then begins to rise. What does the point where it starts to rise represent?
cards.a: The renal threshold.
options: The transport maximum
The renal threshold
The filtered load
The splay
cards.explanation: The plasma concentration where glucose first shows up in urine is the renal threshold, which is reached before the transport maximum because some nephrons saturate earlier than others. The transport maximum is where the reabsorption curve flattens, at a higher plasma concentration. Filtered load is the rising straight line of delivery, and splay is the rounded region between threshold and maximum rather than a single point.

cards.q: Plasma glucose is 600 mg/dL, GFR is 100 mL/min, and the transport maximum for glucose is 375 mg/min. How much glucose is excreted per minute?
cards.a: 225 mg/min.
options: 125 mg/min
600 mg/min
375 mg/min
225 mg/min
cards.explanation: The filtered load is 6 mg/mL times 100 mL/min, or 600 mg/min. Carriers reclaim 375 mg/min, so 600 minus 375 leaves 225 mg/min in the urine. Six hundred is the filtered load, which would only all be excreted if reabsorption were zero, and 375 is the reabsorbed amount. The 125 value comes from a different case with a normal GFR and a plasma glucose of 400 mg/dL.

cards.q: Two people both have a plasma glucose of 500 mg/dL and a normal transport maximum of 375 mg/min. One has a GFR of 125 mL/min and the other has a GFR reduced to 60 mL/min. Compare their glucose excretion.
cards.a: The person with the higher GFR excretes more, and the one with the low GFR may excrete none.
options: Both excrete the same amount, because plasma glucose is equal
The person with the higher GFR excretes more, and the one with the low GFR may excrete none
The person with the lower GFR excretes more, because filtration is impaired
Neither excretes glucose, because the transport maximum is normal in both
cards.explanation: Excretion depends on filtered load compared with capacity. At a GFR of 125 mL/min the filtered load is 625 mg/min, which exceeds 375 and leaves 250 mg/min in the urine, while at 60 mL/min the load is only 300 mg/min, which the carriers can fully reclaim. Equal plasma glucose does not mean equal delivery once GFR differs. A low GFR delivers less glucose, not more, and normal capacity does not prevent spillage when delivery is high.

cards.q: In uncontrolled hyperglycemia, glucose that exceeds the transport maximum remains in the tubular fluid. Trace what this does to water handling and then to the person's thirst.
cards.a: Retained glucose holds water in the tubule, urine volume rises, body water falls, and thirst increases.
options: Retained glucose holds water in the tubule, urine volume rises, body water falls, and thirst increases
Retained glucose draws water out of the tubule, urine volume falls, and thirst decreases
Retained glucose has no osmotic effect, so urine volume and thirst are unchanged
Retained glucose is reabsorbed later in the collecting duct, so nothing changes
cards.explanation: Unreabsorbed glucose is osmotically active and holds water in the lumen, producing osmotic diuresis, and the resulting loss of body water raises plasma osmolarity and stimulates thirst. Solute in the tubule pulls water toward itself rather than out of the lumen. Glucose is a strong osmotic particle, so no effect is not an option. The collecting duct has no glucose carriers, so glucose escaping the proximal tubule is lost in the urine.

cards.q: A drug lowers the transport maximum for glucose from 375 mg/min to 150 mg/min. With a GFR of 125 mL/min and a plasma glucose of 200 mg/dL, how much glucose is excreted per minute?
cards.a: 100 mg/min.
options: 50 mg/min
100 mg/min
250 mg/min
0 mg/min
cards.explanation: The filtered load is 2 mg/mL times 125 mL/min, or 250 mg/min, and only 150 mg/min can now be reabsorbed, so 100 mg/min is excreted. Zero would be right with the normal maximum of 375, which is the point of the comparison. The 250 value is the filtered load before any reabsorption, and 50 comes from subtracting in the wrong direction.

cards.q: Which form of endocytosis takes in large solid particles such as bacteria and cell debris?
cards.a: Phagocytosis.
options: Exocytosis
Pinocytosis
Phagocytosis
Receptor mediated endocytosis
cards.explanation: Phagocytosis extends pseudopods around a solid particle and encloses it in a large vesicle, which is how a macrophage clears a bacterium. Pinocytosis takes in droplets of extracellular fluid, not solid particles. Receptor mediated endocytosis takes in specific molecules bound to surface receptors. Exocytosis moves material out of the cell rather than in.

cards.q: Pinocytosis brings which kind of cargo into the cell?
cards.a: Small droplets of extracellular fluid and whatever is dissolved in them.
options: Only lipid soluble hormones
Solid particles the size of bacteria
Small droplets of extracellular fluid and whatever is dissolved in them
Only molecules bound to specific surface receptors
cards.explanation: Pinocytosis, sometimes called cell drinking, pinches off small vesicles of extracellular fluid, so the cargo is whatever happens to be dissolved nearby and the process is nonselective. Solid particles of bacterial size go by phagocytosis. Selection by receptor is receptor mediated endocytosis. Lipid soluble hormones cross the bilayer directly and need no vesicle at all.

cards.q: Which protein coats the membrane pit that forms during receptor mediated endocytosis?
cards.a: Clathrin.
options: Myosin
Tubulin
Actin
Clathrin
cards.explanation: Clathrin assembles into a cage on the cytosolic face of the pit and helps curve the membrane into a vesicle, which is why these are called clathrin coated pits. Actin and myosin generate movement and shape change more broadly, including the pseudopods of phagocytosis, but they are not the coat here. Tubulin builds microtubules that carry vesicles once they have formed.

cards.q: Which particle is the classic example of cargo taken up by receptor mediated endocytosis?
cards.a: Low density lipoprotein.
options: Low density lipoprotein
Oxygen
Na+
Carbon dioxide
cards.explanation: LDL binds to specific LDL receptors that gather in coated pits, which is how cells obtain cholesterol from the blood. Oxygen and carbon dioxide are small nonpolar gases that diffuse straight through the bilayer. Na+ crosses through channels and transporters. None of those three needs a vesicle, and none binds a receptor for uptake.

cards.q: What does exocytosis accomplish?
cards.a: It fuses a vesicle with the plasma membrane and releases the contents.
options: It moves single molecules through a channel in the membrane
It engulfs bacteria and debris into a large vesicle
It fuses a vesicle with the plasma membrane and releases the contents
It pulls droplets of extracellular fluid into the cell
cards.explanation: In exocytosis a secretory vesicle merges with the plasma membrane, so its contents empty into the extracellular fluid without ever crossing the bilayer. Engulfing bacteria is phagocytosis and taking in fluid is pinocytosis, both of which move material inward. Channel transport moves individual dissolved solutes and cannot handle proteins or packaged transmitter.

cards.q: Which ion entering an axon terminal triggers exocytosis of neurotransmitter?
cards.a: Ca2+.
options: Na+
K+
Ca2+
Cl-
cards.explanation: Ca2+ entering through voltage gated calcium channels binds the vesicle sensor protein and sets off fusion, which is why blocking Ca2+ entry silences transmitter release. Na+ entry carries the depolarization that opens those calcium channels, but Na+ is not the fusion trigger itself, which is the most common mix up here. K+ efflux repolarizes the terminal, and Cl- is not part of this release step.

cards.q: How much ATP does vesicular transport require?
cards.a: ATP is required, because membrane remodeling and vesicle movement need energy.
options: ATP is required, because membrane remodeling and vesicle movement need energy
ATP is required only for exocytosis and not for any form of endocytosis
ATP is required only when the cargo is a charged molecule
None, because vesicles move passively down gradients
cards.explanation: Bending membrane, assembling coats, moving vesicles along the cytoskeleton, and driving fusion all consume ATP, so every form of vesicular transport is an active process. Vesicles do not follow concentration gradients, so calling the process passive misses the point. Endocytosis is just as energy dependent as exocytosis, and the cost has nothing to do with whether the cargo carries a charge.

cards.q: Which family of proteins catalyzes the fusion of a secretory vesicle with the plasma membrane?
cards.a: SNARE proteins.
options: Aquaporins
Cadherins
SNARE proteins
Integrins
cards.explanation: SNARE proteins on the vesicle and on the target membrane zipper together and pull the two bilayers close enough to fuse. Integrins anchor cells to the extracellular matrix, and cadherins hold neighboring cells together, so both are adhesion proteins rather than fusion machinery. Aquaporins are water channels and play no role in vesicle fusion.

cards.q: A neutrophil extends pseudopods around a bacterium and encloses it in a vesicle. Which process is this?
cards.a: Phagocytosis.
options: Exocytosis
Pinocytosis
Receptor mediated endocytosis
Phagocytosis
cards.explanation: Surrounding a large solid target with pseudopods and sealing it into a vesicle is phagocytosis, the specialty of neutrophils and macrophages. Pinocytosis brings in fluid droplets rather than particles this large. Receptor mediated endocytosis concentrates specific molecules in coated pits and does not use pseudopods. Exocytosis would send material outward instead.

cards.q: A liver cell binds LDL particles to surface receptors that cluster in coated pits, then internalizes them. Which process is this?
cards.a: Receptor mediated endocytosis.
options: Receptor mediated endocytosis
Phagocytosis
Pinocytosis
Simple diffusion
cards.explanation: Binding to a specific receptor and concentrating in a coated pit before internalization defines receptor mediated endocytosis, which lets the cell gather scarce cargo efficiently. Phagocytosis handles large particles with pseudopods and is not receptor selective in this way. Pinocytosis is nonselective fluid uptake. A lipoprotein particle is far too large to diffuse through the bilayer.

cards.q: Voltage gated Ca2+ channels at a nerve terminal are blocked while the action potential still arrives. Predict neurotransmitter release.
cards.a: Release falls sharply, because Ca2+ entry is the trigger for vesicle fusion.
options: Release is unchanged, because depolarization alone triggers fusion
Release falls sharply, because Ca2+ entry is the trigger for vesicle fusion
Release reverses, and transmitter is taken back into the vesicle
Release increases, because the terminal stays depolarized longer
cards.explanation: Depolarization normally works by opening calcium channels, and it is the Ca2+ that binds the vesicle sensor and triggers fusion, so with the channels blocked the vesicles stay put. Longer depolarization does not help when the trigger ion cannot enter. Believing depolarization alone is sufficient is the common misconception this card targets. Exocytosis is not a reversible step in this sense.

cards.q: A cell is treated so that ATP production stops. Which process continues at close to its normal rate?
cards.a: Diffusion of oxygen across the membrane.
options: Phagocytosis of bacteria
Exocytosis of secretory granules
Receptor mediated endocytosis of LDL
Diffusion of oxygen across the membrane
cards.explanation: Oxygen crosses by simple diffusion down its own partial pressure gradient, so it needs no cellular energy. All three vesicular processes require ATP for membrane remodeling, coat assembly, and fusion, so each of them slows or stops when ATP is gone. That shared energy requirement is what groups them together as active transport.

cards.q: A person's cells lack functional LDL receptors. Predict what happens to LDL in the blood.
cards.a: LDL rises, because cells can no longer clear it efficiently by receptor mediated endocytosis.
options: LDL rises, because cells can no longer clear it efficiently by receptor mediated endocytosis
LDL is unchanged, because LDL diffuses into cells through the bilayer
LDL rises only after the cells stop making ATP
LDL falls, because cells take it in by pinocytosis instead
cards.explanation: Receptor mediated endocytosis is the main route by which cells remove LDL from plasma, so losing the receptor leaves LDL circulating and plasma levels climb. Pinocytosis is far too slow and nonselective to substitute. An LDL particle is a large lipid protein complex and cannot diffuse through the membrane. The problem is the missing receptor, not an energy shortage.

cards.q: Which vesicular process is the most selective about what it brings into the cell?
cards.a: Receptor mediated endocytosis, because cargo must bind a specific receptor first.
options: Phagocytosis, because the particles are large
Receptor mediated endocytosis, because cargo must bind a specific receptor first
Exocytosis, because it chooses which granules to release
Pinocytosis, because it samples fluid continuously
cards.explanation: Requiring the cargo to fit a specific receptor makes receptor mediated endocytosis highly selective and lets a cell concentrate a molecule present at low levels outside. Pinocytosis takes whatever is dissolved nearby, which is the opposite of selective. Phagocytosis targets particles but is far less molecule specific. Exocytosis moves cargo out and therefore is not an uptake route at all.

cards.q: Botulinum toxin cleaves SNARE proteins in motor nerve terminals. Trace the effect on acetylcholine release and then on the muscle.
cards.a: Vesicles cannot fuse, acetylcholine release fails, and the muscle becomes weak or paralyzed.
options: Ca2+ entry stops, so acetylcholine is released without a trigger
Vesicles cannot fuse, acetylcholine release fails, and the muscle becomes weak or paralyzed
Vesicles fuse faster, acetylcholine floods the synapse, and the muscle contracts continuously
Vesicles fuse normally but acetylcholine is destroyed, so the muscle is unaffected
cards.explanation: SNARE proteins are the fusion machinery, so cleaving them leaves docked vesicles unable to merge with the membrane and the terminal cannot release transmitter, which leaves the muscle unstimulated and flaccid. Destroying the fusion machinery cannot increase release. If release failed, the muscle would certainly be affected. The claim that stopping Ca2+ entry causes release without a trigger contradicts itself.

cards.q: A mutation prevents clathrin coated pits from forming but leaves membrane ruffling and pseudopod formation intact. Predict which processes fail and which continue.
cards.a: Receptor mediated endocytosis fails while phagocytosis and pinocytosis continue.
options: Only exocytosis fails, because vesicles cannot leave the Golgi
Receptor mediated endocytosis fails while phagocytosis and pinocytosis continue
All forms of endocytosis fail together
Phagocytosis fails while receptor mediated endocytosis continues
cards.explanation: Clathrin builds the coat that curves the pit in receptor mediated endocytosis, so that route is lost, while phagocytosis and pinocytosis rely on actin driven membrane movement that the mutation spares. That difference is exactly why the three routes are studied as separate mechanisms. Phagocytosis does not depend on clathrin, and exocytosis uses SNARE mediated fusion rather than clathrin coated pits at the plasma membrane.

cards.q: A pancreatic cell releases secretory granules by exocytosis at a high rate for hours, yet its surface area does not keep growing. What accounts for this?
cards.a: The added membrane is retrieved by endocytosis and recycled to form new vesicles.
options: The added membrane is digested by extracellular enzymes
Exocytosis does not add membrane, because the vesicle contents pass through a pore only
The cell divides each time its surface area increases
The added membrane is retrieved by endocytosis and recycled to form new vesicles
cards.explanation: Every fusion event adds vesicle membrane to the cell surface, and cells balance that by pulling equivalent membrane back in as endocytic vesicles, so surface area stays roughly constant and membrane components are reused. Extracellular digestion of the cell's own membrane would breach the barrier. Full fusion genuinely inserts the vesicle membrane, and cell division is far too slow and drastic to serve as membrane bookkeeping.

cards.q: In a cell line, endosomes fail to acidify after internalization, so receptors and their bound ligands do not separate. Predict the effect on receptor recycling and on further uptake of that ligand.
cards.a: Receptors are not returned to the surface, so uptake of the ligand declines over time.
options: Uptake continues unchanged, because ligand enters by pinocytosis instead
Receptors are not returned to the surface, so uptake of the ligand declines over time
Receptors return to the surface faster, so uptake rises over time
Receptors are unaffected, because separation happens at the cell surface
cards.explanation: The drop in endosomal pH is what makes the receptor release its ligand so the receptor can be shuttled back to the plasma membrane for another round. Without that separation, receptors are trapped with their cargo, surface receptor numbers fall, and uptake declines. Failing to release cargo cannot speed recycling. Separation occurs inside the endosome, not at the surface, and pinocytosis is far too slow to replace a receptor based route.

cards.q: In a polarized epithelial cell, the apical membrane faces which compartment?
cards.a: The lumen.
options: The adjacent epithelial cell
The lumen
The interstitial fluid
The capillary blood
cards.explanation: The apical surface is the one exposed to the lumen, such as the inside of the intestine or the kidney tubule, and it is where absorbed material first enters the cell. Interstitial fluid and blood lie on the other side, which is served by the basolateral membrane. The surface contacting a neighboring cell is the lateral membrane and is where junctions form.

cards.q: The basolateral membrane of an intestinal epithelial cell faces which compartment?
cards.a: The interstitial fluid on the blood side.
options: The interstitial fluid on the blood side
The lumen of a secretory vesicle
The inside of the nucleus
The gut lumen
cards.explanation: The basolateral membrane lines the sides and base of the cell and faces the interstitial fluid, so solutes crossing there are on their way into the blood. The lumen is served by the apical membrane on the opposite face. Vesicle membranes are internal compartments, and the nucleus is not part of the transport route across an epithelium.

cards.q: In an intestinal or proximal tubule cell, where is the SGLT sodium glucose cotransporter located?
cards.a: The apical membrane.
options: The mitochondrial inner membrane
The basolateral membrane
The apical membrane
The nuclear envelope
cards.explanation: SGLT sits on the apical membrane, which is where it can pull glucose out of the lumen using the inward Na+ gradient. Putting it on the basolateral side would drag glucose from the interstitial fluid instead of absorbing it. The nuclear envelope and mitochondrial membranes handle internal traffic and have nothing to do with transepithelial absorption.

cards.q: Where is GLUT2, the carrier that lets absorbed glucose leave the epithelial cell, located?
cards.a: The basolateral membrane.
options: In the tight junction itself
The apical membrane
The basolateral membrane
Both membranes equally
cards.explanation: GLUT2 is basolateral, so glucose that has accumulated inside the cell can move down its gradient toward the interstitial fluid and blood. If GLUT2 were apical, absorbed glucose would leak straight back into the lumen. Equal distribution would defeat the whole point of polarity, and tight junctions are sealing structures, not transport proteins.

cards.q: In a polarized absorptive epithelial cell, where is the Na+/K+ ATPase found?
cards.a: Only on the basolateral membrane.
options: Only in the tight junction
Only on the apical membrane
Only on the basolateral membrane
Evenly on both membranes
cards.explanation: The pump is restricted to the basolateral membrane, where it moves absorbed Na+ toward the blood and, by keeping intracellular Na+ low, maintains the gradient that apical carriers depend on. An apical pump would push Na+ back into the lumen. An even distribution would cancel any net direction of transport, and junction proteins do not pump ions.

cards.q: What do tight junctions between epithelial cells accomplish?
cards.a: They seal the space between cells and keep the two membrane domains distinct.
options: They supply ATP to nearby membrane transporters
They pump Na+ from the lumen into the cell using ATP
They seal the space between cells and keep the two membrane domains distinct
They open wide to allow proteins to pass into the blood
cards.explanation: Tight junctions seal the space between neighboring cells and act as a fence that prevents membrane proteins from drifting between the apical and basolateral domains, which is what makes directional transport possible. They do not transport ions themselves, so pumping is not their role. They restrict rather than permit protein passage, and they have no role in energy supply.

cards.q: What is transcellular transport?
cards.a: Movement of solute through the cells, crossing both the apical and basolateral membranes.
options: Movement of solute inside a blood vessel
Movement of solute through the cells, crossing both the apical and basolateral membranes
Movement of solute between adjacent cells through the tight junction
Movement of solute along the surface of the epithelium
cards.explanation: Transcellular means through the cell, so the solute enters at one membrane and exits at the other, which is the route glucose takes during absorption. Slipping between cells is the paracellular route. Movement along the surface is not transport across the epithelium at all, and flow inside a vessel is bulk transport rather than membrane transport.

cards.q: What does it mean to say an epithelium is polarized?
cards.a: The apical and basolateral membranes contain different transport proteins.
options: The apical and basolateral membranes contain different transport proteins
The cells are aligned with the magnetic field of the body
All the cells face the same direction but have identical membranes
The cells carry a net electrical charge on one side
cards.explanation: Polarity means the two faces of the cell are equipped differently, and that difference in transporters is what allows solute to move in one direction across the sheet. A net charge on one side describes a membrane potential rather than polarity in this sense. Magnetic alignment is not a physiological concept. Identical membranes would give no net direction, which is exactly what polarity provides.

cards.q: Glucose enters an intestinal epithelial cell from the lumen. Which type of transport is that first step?
cards.a: Secondary active transport.
options: Facilitated diffusion
Secondary active transport
Primary active transport
Simple diffusion
cards.explanation: Glucose is carried in by SGLT together with Na+, using the Na+ gradient rather than ATP, which makes the apical step secondary active transport and lets glucose move against its own gradient. Facilitated diffusion happens later, at the basolateral membrane through GLUT2. Simple diffusion cannot move polar glucose, and primary active transport would require the carrier itself to hydrolyze ATP.

cards.q: Glucose leaves the epithelial cell across the basolateral membrane on its way to the blood. Which type of transport is that step?
cards.a: Facilitated diffusion through GLUT2.
options: Facilitated diffusion through GLUT2
Secondary active transport through SGLT
Primary active transport by an ATPase
Vesicular transport by exocytosis
cards.explanation: Apical uptake concentrates glucose inside the cell, so glucose can then move downhill through GLUT2, a passive carrier that needs no energy. SGLT is on the apical side and works in the opposite direction. No ATPase carries glucose, and packaging glucose into vesicles would be a wasteful way to move a small sugar.

cards.q: Phlorizin blocks apical SGLT in the proximal tubule. Predict the effect on glucose reabsorption from the tubular fluid.
cards.a: Reabsorption falls, because glucose can no longer be pulled out of the lumen.
options: Reabsorption falls, because glucose can no longer be pulled out of the lumen
Reabsorption is unchanged, because glucose crosses the apical membrane by diffusion
Reabsorption reverses, and glucose is pumped from blood into the cell
Reabsorption rises, because GLUT2 compensates
cards.explanation: The apical step is the entry point for the entire pathway, so blocking SGLT strands glucose in the tubular fluid and it is excreted. GLUT2 sits on the basolateral membrane and cannot reach luminal glucose. Glucose is polar and does not cross the apical membrane by simple diffusion. Blocking a carrier does not create transport in the opposite direction.

cards.q: Ouabain is applied only to the basolateral side of an intestinal epithelium. Predict the effect on glucose uptake at the apical membrane.
cards.a: It falls, because the Na+ gradient that drives apical SGLT is lost.
options: It falls only if glucose is also removed from the lumen
It rises, because Na+ inside the cell increases
It falls, because the Na+ gradient that drives apical SGLT is lost
It is unchanged, because ouabain acts only on the side where it is applied
cards.explanation: The basolateral Na+/K+ ATPase keeps intracellular Na+ low, and that low internal Na+ is what makes the apical Na+ gradient steep enough to power SGLT. Blocking the pump on one side therefore shuts down transport on the other side, which shows how the two membranes work as one system. Rising intracellular Na+ weakens rather than strengthens the driving force, and luminal glucose is not the limiting factor here.

cards.q: Which membrane of an absorptive epithelial cell holds the transporter that keeps intracellular Na+ low?
cards.a: The basolateral membrane.
options: The basolateral membrane
Both membranes equally
Neither, since Na+ is kept low by binding proteins in the cytosol
The apical membrane
cards.explanation: The basolateral Na+/K+ ATPase exports Na+ toward the interstitial fluid, which is what holds cytosolic Na+ low and sustains apical Na+ coupled uptake. An apical pump would return Na+ to the lumen and defeat absorption. Equal distribution would eliminate directionality, and cytosolic binding proteins are not how cells maintain their Na+ gradient.

cards.q: Sodium is absorbed across an intestinal epithelium and water follows. What drives the water movement?
cards.a: Water follows the osmotic gradient created by solute absorption.
options: Water is carried inside vesicles with the Na+
Water moves because tight junctions actively squeeze it through
Water is pumped by an ATP driven water pump
Water follows the osmotic gradient created by solute absorption
cards.explanation: Moving Na+ and its accompanying solutes to the blood side raises osmolarity there, and water follows passively through aquaporins and between cells. There is no water pump in human cell membranes, since water movement is always driven by osmotic and hydrostatic forces.
