Vesicular carriage would be far too slow for the volumes involved, and junctions are passive seals rather than motors.

cards.q: Na+ moves from the lumen into an intestinal epithelial cell across the apical membrane. Relative to its electrochemical gradient, how does Na+ move at that step?
cards.a: Downhill, because intracellular Na+ is low and the cell interior is negative.
options: Uphill, which is why ATP is required at the apical membrane
Neither, because Na+ is at equilibrium across the apical membrane
Uphill, powered by the glucose gradient
Downhill, because intracellular Na+ is low and the cell interior is negative
cards.explanation: The basolateral pump keeps intracellular Na+ low and the inside of the cell negative, so Na+ entering from the lumen is moving downhill and releases energy. That released energy is what SGLT harnesses to carry glucose uphill. No ATP is spent at the apical membrane. Na+ is far from equilibrium there, and it is Na+ that powers glucose transport, not the reverse.

cards.q: Put the steps of glucose absorption in the correct order from gut lumen to blood.
cards.a: SGLT at the apical membrane, then GLUT2 at the basolateral membrane, then the capillary.
options: Na+/K+ ATPase at the apical membrane, then SGLT at the basolateral membrane, then the capillary
Simple diffusion across both membranes, then the capillary
GLUT2 at the apical membrane, then SGLT at the basolateral membrane, then the capillary
SGLT at the apical membrane, then GLUT2 at the basolateral membrane, then the capillary
cards.explanation: Glucose is pulled from the lumen by apical SGLT using the Na+ gradient, accumulates inside the cell, and then exits downhill through basolateral GLUT2 into the interstitial fluid, from which it enters the capillary. Swapping the two carriers puts each on the wrong face and would move glucose out of the blood instead of into it. The pump is basolateral, and glucose is too polar to diffuse through either membrane.

cards.q: A toxin blocks basolateral GLUT2 in an intestinal epithelial cell while apical SGLT stays intact. Predict what happens to intracellular glucose and then to apical glucose uptake.
cards.a: Intracellular glucose rises, and apical uptake slows as the internal gradient steepens.
options: Intracellular glucose rises, and apical uptake speeds up to compensate
Intracellular glucose is unchanged, because SGLT stops immediately
Intracellular glucose rises, and apical uptake slows as the internal gradient steepens
Intracellular glucose falls, and apical uptake speeds up to compensate
cards.explanation: With its exit blocked, glucose piles up in the cytosol, and SGLT then has to push glucose against an increasingly steep internal gradient, so uptake slows even though the carrier is undamaged. Glucose cannot fall when entry continues and exit is blocked. There is no mechanism by which a rising internal load speeds the apical carrier, and SGLT does not stop the instant GLUT2 is blocked, so intracellular glucose does change.

cards.q: Suppose an epithelial cell mistakenly placed its Na+/K+ ATPase in the apical membrane instead of the basolateral membrane. Predict the effect on net Na+ absorption from the lumen.
cards.a: Net Na+ absorption would fail, because the pump would push Na+ back into the lumen.
options: Net absorption would be unchanged, because the pump works the same on either face
Na+ would be absorbed but glucose would not
Net absorption would rise, because the pump would be closer to the lumen
Net Na+ absorption would fail, because the pump would push Na+ back into the lumen
cards.explanation: The pump always moves Na+ from cytosol to the side it faces, so an apical pump would return absorbed Na+ to the lumen and no net transfer to the blood would occur. Proximity to the lumen does not help when the direction of pumping is wrong. Location is exactly what determines the direction of transepithelial transport, so this could never be a neutral change, and glucose uptake would also fail once the Na+ gradient collapsed.

cards.q: Cholera toxin causes intestinal cells to secrete Cl- across the apical membrane at a high rate. Trace what happens next to Na+ and to water in the lumen.
cards.a: Na+ follows Cl- into the lumen and water follows osmotically, producing watery diarrhea.
options: Na+ moves into the blood and water follows it, so the stool becomes dry
Na+ stays in the cell and water moves into the blood
Only Cl- accumulates in the lumen, since water cannot cross the epithelium
Na+ follows Cl- into the lumen and water follows osmotically, producing watery diarrhea
cards.explanation: Secreted Cl- makes the lumen electrically negative, so Na+ follows through the paracellular route, and the added NaCl raises luminal osmolarity so water is pulled in as well, which is the mechanism of secretory diarrhea. Absorption into the blood is the opposite of what secretion does. Na+ does not sit trapped in the cell, and the epithelium is highly water permeable, which is precisely why the fluid loss is so large.

cards.q: In a membrane transport simulation, which transport type stops when a metabolic poison removes ATP from the model cell?
cards.a: Active transport.
options: Active transport
Osmosis of water
Simple diffusion
Facilitated diffusion
cards.explanation: Only active transport spends ATP, so it is the one process the poison shuts down. Simple and facilitated diffusion run on the solute gradient and keep going, which is why the poison run is the standard test for distinguishing them. Osmosis is likewise passive and follows the water gradient regardless of ATP.

cards.q: In the simulation, which transport type shows no plateau no matter how high the solute concentration is raised?
cards.a: Simple diffusion.
options: Primary active transport
Secondary active transport
Simple diffusion
Facilitated diffusion
cards.explanation: Simple diffusion has no carriers to saturate, so its rate keeps rising as long as the gradient rises. All three of the other processes depend on a limited number of transport proteins, so each one flattens into a plateau once every binding site is occupied. Watching for that plateau is how the simulation separates protein mediated transport from movement through the lipid.

cards.q: In the simulation, the concentration gradient for a passively transported solute is reversed. What happens to the direction of net movement?
cards.a: It reverses, because passive transport always follows the gradient.
options: It stays the same, because carriers have a fixed direction
It reverses, because passive transport always follows the gradient
It stops permanently
It becomes random with no net direction at any concentration
cards.explanation: Passive transport has no preferred direction, so flipping which side has more solute flips the direction of net flux. Carriers used in facilitated diffusion are not one way valves. Transport does not stop, since a gradient still exists, and net movement is only zero when the two sides are equal, not whenever the gradient is reversed.

cards.q: In the simulation, what is the defining behavior of active transport that neither type of diffusion shows?
cards.a: It can move solute uphill, from the low side to the high side.
options: It works only at a temperature of 37 C
It can move solute uphill, from the low side to the high side
It moves solute faster than diffusion at every concentration
It requires a membrane containing wide open pores
cards.explanation: Moving solute uphill against its gradient is the behavior that requires an energy input, and it is what marks a run as active transport. Speed alone does not distinguish the processes, since an open channel can outpace a pump. Pores are features of channels, which are passive, and temperature affects all of the processes rather than defining any one of them.

cards.q: What is the purpose of running a control condition in the transport simulation?
cards.a: To provide a baseline rate against which the treated runs are compared.
options: To confirm that the solute is present
To increase the transport rate in later runs
To make the membrane thicker for later trials
To provide a baseline rate against which the treated runs are compared
cards.explanation: The control gives the untreated transport rate, so any change seen after adding poison, reversing the gradient, or changing carrier number can be attributed to that one variable. Confirming the solute is present is a setup check, not the reason for a control. A control does not alter later runs, and it does not change the properties of the simulated membrane.

cards.q: You build a curve of transport rate against solute concentration in the simulation. Which variable is the independent variable?
cards.a: The solute concentration you set.
options: The number of carriers in the membrane
The temperature of the bath
The transport rate
The solute concentration you set
cards.explanation: The independent variable is the one you set on purpose, which here is the solute concentration plotted along the horizontal axis. Transport rate is the dependent variable, since it is the outcome you measure. Carrier number and temperature are held constant in this particular run, which makes them controlled variables rather than the independent one.

cards.q: In the simulation, which factor does not affect the rate of simple diffusion of a solute across the membrane?
cards.a: The number of carrier proteins in the membrane.
options: The surface area of the membrane
The lipid solubility of the solute
The number of carrier proteins in the membrane
The size of the concentration gradient
cards.explanation: Simple diffusion goes straight through the lipid, so carrier number is irrelevant to it, and adding carriers changes only the carrier mediated runs. The gradient sets the driving force, larger surface area gives more room to cross, and greater lipid solubility lets the solute dissolve into the bilayer more readily, so all three of those do change the rate.

cards.q: In the simulation, which two transport types require a transport protein to be present in the model membrane?
cards.a: Facilitated diffusion and active transport.
options: Simple diffusion and facilitated diffusion
Osmosis and active transport only
Simple diffusion and osmosis
Facilitated diffusion and active transport
cards.explanation: Facilitated diffusion needs a carrier or channel, and active transport needs a pump, so removing the protein sets both rates to zero. Simple diffusion needs no protein at all, which is why it is the process that continues in a bare lipid membrane. Osmosis of water can occur through the lipid as well, though aquaporins speed it up.

cards.q: In a simulation run, a solute continues to move from the compartment with the lower concentration into the compartment with the higher concentration. What does this tell you about the transport?
cards.a: It is active transport, since energy is moving solute uphill.
options: It is facilitated diffusion through a carrier protein
It is active transport, since energy is moving solute uphill
It is osmosis of water across the membrane
It is simple diffusion through the lipid bilayer
cards.explanation: Uphill movement cannot occur without an energy input, so a run that builds a gradient rather than erasing one must be active transport. Both forms of diffusion stop at equal concentrations and can never push past that point. Osmosis describes water movement, not the solute movement measured here.

cards.q: In a simulation run, doubling the solute gradient doubles the transport rate, and the rate keeps rising with no ceiling at any concentration tested. Which process is this?
cards.a: Simple diffusion.
options: Simple diffusion
Facilitated diffusion
Primary active transport
Secondary active transport
cards.explanation: A rate that rises in direct proportion with no ceiling means nothing is saturating, which points to movement through the lipid rather than through a limited set of proteins. Facilitated diffusion would flatten once the carriers were full. Both active transport types would also flatten and would require energy, which a strictly gradient driven result does not indicate.

cards.q: A metabolic poison is added in the simulation and the transport rate for solute X does not change. Which conclusion is best supported?
cards.a: Solute X is moving by a passive process.
options: Solute X is being actively transported
Solute X is moving by a passive process
Solute X must be crossing without any protein
Solute X is being moved against its gradient
cards.explanation: Insensitivity to ATP loss rules out active transport and marks the process as passive, but the poison test alone cannot say whether the passive route is simple or facilitated diffusion. Deciding between those two requires the saturation test. Uphill movement is also ruled out, since a passive process cannot build a gradient.

cards.q: In the simulation you increase the number of carrier proteins in the membrane while keeping the solute concentration high enough to saturate them. Predict the effect on the transport rate.
cards.a: The maximum rate rises, because more carriers can work at once.
options: The maximum rate falls, because carriers interfere with each other
The rate is unchanged, because saturation is already reached
The rate becomes linear with concentration
The maximum rate rises, because more carriers can work at once
cards.explanation: The saturated rate is the sum of what all carriers can move, so adding carriers raises the ceiling. Carriers in the same membrane operate independently and do not obstruct each other. Saturation limits the carriers that were already present, not the new ones. The curve keeps its saturating shape, since more carriers only shift the plateau upward.

cards.q: In the simulation you double the surface area of the membrane while holding the concentration gradient constant. Predict the effect on the rate of simple diffusion.
cards.a: It roughly doubles.
options: It is unchanged, because the gradient did not change
It falls to zero
It roughly doubles
It is halved
cards.explanation: Diffusion rate is proportional to the area available for crossing, so twice the area gives roughly twice the flux even with the same driving gradient. Adding area cannot slow diffusion or stop it. Saying nothing changes ignores area as a determinant, which is exactly the variable this run isolates.

cards.q: In the simulation, the pore size of a channel is set smaller than the solute molecule. Predict the transport rate for that solute through the channel.
cards.a: It falls to essentially zero, because the solute cannot fit through the pore.
options: It stays the same, because pore size affects only water
It falls to essentially zero, because the solute cannot fit through the pore
It reverses direction
It rises, because the solute is forced through faster
cards.explanation: A channel is a size selective pore, so a solute larger than the opening simply cannot pass and flux through that route drops to nearly nothing. Narrowing a pore cannot accelerate passage. Pore size restricts every solute, not only water, and blocking a path does not create movement in the opposite direction.

cards.q: In the simulation, solute X shows these results: the transport rate plateaus at high concentration, a metabolic poison does not change it, and reversing the gradient reverses the direction of net movement. Which transport type is solute X using?
cards.a: Facilitated diffusion.
options: Simple diffusion
Facilitated diffusion
Primary active transport
Osmosis
cards.explanation: The plateau shows a limited number of transport proteins, while ATP independence and gradient following both show the process is passive, which together identify facilitated diffusion. Simple diffusion is ruled out by the plateau. Active transport is ruled out by the poison result and by the willingness to reverse with the gradient. Osmosis refers to water rather than a solute.

cards.q: In the simulation, solute Y shows these results: the transport rate plateaus at high concentration, a metabolic poison stops transport, and the solute continues to move into the compartment that already has more of it. Which transport type is solute Y using?
cards.a: Active transport.
options: Active transport
Movement through a leaky junction
Simple diffusion
Facilitated diffusion
cards.explanation: Uphill movement plus dependence on ATP identifies active transport, and the plateau confirms a limited number of pump proteins. Simple diffusion would neither plateau nor need ATP. Facilitated diffusion plateaus but is ATP independent and cannot build a gradient. A leak pathway is passive and would erase the gradient rather than deepen it.

cards.q: Two solutes both plateau at high concentration in the simulation, so both are protein mediated. Which single additional run best separates facilitated diffusion from active transport?
cards.a: Add the metabolic poison and see which transport stops.
options: Add more solute to the high concentration side
Raise the temperature of the bath
Add the metabolic poison and see which transport stops
Increase the surface area of the membrane
cards.explanation: Active transport depends on ATP and facilitated diffusion does not, so the poison run separates them cleanly in a single test. Temperature speeds up both processes and distinguishes neither. Extra membrane area raises both rates. Adding still more solute only confirms the plateau you have already seen, which both processes share.

cards.q: In the simulation a student sees a solute moving into the compartment that already has more of it, even though ATP is not being supplied to the transport protein itself. What is the best explanation?
cards.a: A coupled carrier is using another solute's gradient, so this is secondary active transport.
options: The simulation is measuring simple diffusion through the lipid bilayer
The transport protein is producing its own ATP as it carries the solute
The gradient in the simulation must actually point the other way
A coupled carrier is using another solute's gradient, so this is secondary active transport
cards.explanation: A carrier can move one solute uphill by letting a second solute run downhill, so no ATP touches the protein even though the process is still active transport, one step removed from the pump that built the driver gradient. Simple diffusion could never move solute uphill. Transport proteins consume energy rather than producing ATP, and dismissing the observed gradient avoids the question instead of explaining it.
